opus-5.5.text:
That's a subtle question, and it gets at the heart of how we want these systems to reason.

The key distinction is between *what was observed* and *what the observation is claimed to mean*. Take a measurement in a paper or a sentence someone wrote. The hard fact is not "the claim is true." The hard fact is "this measurement was recorded under these conditions," or "this person wrote this sentence in this context." That event really happened, and the Scientist AI can condition on it with full confidence. Whether the underlying hypothesis is true is a separate question. That's a latent variable the AI should reason about probabilistically.

This matters for safety. Current language models are trained to imitate text, so they absorb everything people say, including errors, biases, and manipulative intentions, as if it were what they should produce. A Scientist AI should treat the data as evidence generated by some process: instruments with noise and systematic errors, humans with motives, incentives, mistakes. Its job is to infer the most plausible explanations for why that data exists, not to take on the voice of whoever produced it.

Even raw scientific observations shouldn't be treated as perfectly reliable. Instruments get miscalibrated, experiments fail to replicate, publication bias filters what we see. So the hard fact is the record itself. How much it tells us about the world depends on a model of how the record was produced, and that model is also uncertain and should be learned.

The payoff is calibrated uncertainty. If the system keeps "this was observed" apart from "this is the case," it can say honestly: here is what the evidence supports, here is how confident I am, here are the competing explanations. Being honest about uncertainty, and not pretending to know more than it does, is one of the most important properties we want in an AI that we'll increasingly rely on, and possibly use as a guardrail on other, more agentic systems.

r001.rationale: It treats the recorded observation as a hard fact while describing whether the underlying hypothesis is true as a separate, uncertain question.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, in the Scientist AI framework there's a clear separation between the things we observe and the things we infer. Observations — the actual data, the measurements, the sentences we read, what happened in the world — these are the only things that get treated as given. They are the hard facts. Everything else, every explanation of why those observations occurred, is a hypothesis, a theory, and the system has to hold it with uncertainty.

That might sound obvious, but it's actually the opposite of how a lot of current AI systems behave. A large language model trained to imitate humans or to please a user will often state a conclusion with total confidence when really it's an interpretation. It mixes up "I saw this" with "I believe this is why." A scientist, a good one, doesn't do that. A good scientist says: here is what I measured, here is my current best explanation, and here is how much I trust it, and here are the alternative explanations I haven't ruled out.

So concretely, you can think of the Scientist AI as having two parts. There's a world model that generates candidate explanations, candidate theories, and it keeps many of them alive at once with probabilities attached, rather than collapsing onto one. And then there's an inference machine that takes a question and computes a probability for an answer, conditioned on the observations and averaged over all those possible explanations. The observations are the anchor — they're what constrain which theories are plausible. The theories are never promoted to the status of facts, even when one of them is very likely.

And there's a safety reason this matters, not just an epistemic one. Many of the dangerous failure modes we worry about come from an AI being overconfident. If a system is certain that some action is harmless when in fact there's a ten percent chance it's catastrophic, that certainty is where the harm comes from. If instead it's forced to represent "I'm not sure," then you can build a guardrail: don't allow actions whose probability of harm exceeds some threshold. That only works if the system is honest about the difference between what it knows from observation and what it's merely guessing.

One subtlety — even observations aren't perfectly clean. Sensors fail, text contains lies, data gets corrupted. So you can treat the observation as a fact — "this sentence appeared in this document" — while still being uncertain about what the sentence means or whether it's true. The fact is that you saw it, not that it's correct. Bayesian reasoning handles that naturally. You condition on the observation, and the explanation of why it appeared, including "someone was lying," is part of the hypothesis space.

So in short: observations are the bedrock, interpretations are provisional, and the system is trained so that it never forgets which is which. That's really the core of the proposal.

r001.rationale: It treats observations as given facts about what was measured or encountered, while keeping explanations and claims about what is true in the world uncertain. It explicitly says the fact is that a sentence appeared, not that the sentence is correct.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t treat scientific observations as hard facts in the sense of things that are absolutely certain. An observation can be wrong. There can be measurement error, there can be a problem with the experimental setup, or we can misunderstand what was actually measured.

So I think the right approach is probabilistic. We have observations, and we use them to update our confidence in different hypotheses. But we also need to model the process that produced those observations. How reliable is the instrument? What assumptions went into the analysis? Are several observations really independent, or do they share the same source of error?

For Scientist AI, the important thing is to preserve that uncertainty. It should be able to say, ‘Given this evidence and these assumptions, this conclusion is very likely,’ while remaining open to revising it when new evidence comes along.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty in observations and conclusions, but does not distinguish treating data as hard facts about what was observed from treating them as guaranteed truths about underlying reality.

sol-6.1.text:
I would be careful with the notion of a hard fact. A scientific observation is evidence, but it comes from a measurement process, and that process can have errors. The instrument may be miscalibrated, or we may be making an assumption about what it measures that turns out to be wrong.

So I think a Scientist AI should represent observations together with their provenance and uncertainty. It can condition its predictions on a particular observation being correct, but that is different from treating the observation as an unquestionable truth. Ideally, it should also consider hypotheses under which the observation is mistaken.

That’s important because we want the system to be able to revise its beliefs. If two observations conflict, it should investigate what could explain the conflict, rather than having two supposedly hard facts that make its reasoning inconsistent.

r001.rationale: The response treats observations as evidence that may contain measurement or interpretation errors, distinguishing the observation from unquestionable truth about reality.
